newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durables orders rose in April.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durables orders rose in April.

text.p: Strong demand for new transportation equipment helped drive orders for costly manufactured goods up in April, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.
The total value of new orders for durable goods rose 1.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted $175.56 billion -- a third increase in the past four months -- following a revised 2.2 percent drop in March.
Last month's orders increase was slightly stronger than Wall Street economists' forecasts of a 1.3 percent rise, primarily because transportation goods were stronger than anticipated.

"There wasn't as much of a bounceback as one might have anticipated, given the 2.2 percent drop in March," Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., said.
"It's hard to know how much impact the auto strikes had," she added.

Many analysts had predicted that strikes against General Motors Corp. would weaken car and truck production and that bad weather would hurt deliveries. But Commerce said all the transportation industries except those making railroad equipment received stronger orders in April.
The department previously had estimated that March durable goods orders had fallen 2.6 percent, but it revised that figure to a 2.2 percent decline.
Shipments of finished goods gained 1.4 percent during April to $175.56 billion, a fourth consecutive monthly increase after a 0.9 percent March rise.
Order backlogs, however, fell for a second month, down 0.4 percent after an identical decline in March, possibly a sign of softer orders in future.

Orders for durable goods, items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years, can indicate the future strength of the manufacturing sector, which in turn weighs heavily on the overall economy.

Transportation equipment orders rose 4.5 percent to $39.36 billion in April after drops of 3.9 percent in March and 7.2 percent in February. Transportation accounts for more than one-fifth of the value of total durable goods orders.
Analysts said beforehand that aircraft maker Boeing Co. had strong orders in April, but the Commerce Department does not break out aircraft orders separately in the monthly durable-goods report.
Excluding transportation, durables orders increased in April only by 0.5 percent following a 1.7 percent decline in March.
"Aircraft orders have been jumping around quite a bit (recently)," Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co. International Inc., said.
"We had a big decline in transportation orders last month and they bounced back this time. Excluding transportation, it's more a picture of stability."

Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, fell 1.3 percent in April after a 2.9 percent plunge in March. It marked the fifth decline in nondefense orders in the past seven months, another indication that demand may be waning.

"Non-defence capital goods orders were down 1.3 percent and they are the most important component of the release," Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp., said. "It's one of the 10 components of the index of leading economic indicators and it gives you a better sense of the trend of orders. So, on balance this is a positive report."
"There are so many ways to cut these durable goods numbers," Seto said. "Ex-defence and ex-transportation, there is a slight hint of softness. But I don't consider that the start of a trend.
"We'll resume growth (in durable goods orders). The big ticket items are always difficult to predict, but overall capital spending will continue to show moderate growth."
Orders for electronic and electrical goods decreased in April by 5.3 percent to $27.26 billion following a 6 percent drop in March. The department said orders weakened for communications equipment.
But orders for industrial machinery, which includes computers, were up 2.2 percent to $33.94 billion after a slight 0.2 percent gain in March.
Orders for primary metals increased 2.8 percent to $16.45 billion after a 1.2 percent March rise.
